title: Stuffed shells, cheese-filled, with meat sauce

content.title: About
content.content: Stuffed shells are large pasta shells filled with a blend of ricotta, mozzarella and parmesan cheeses, baked under a rich meat sauce made from ground beef, tomatoes and aromatic herbs. The dish is a staple of Italian cuisine and is often served as a hearty lunch or dinner.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Traditionally the shells are filled by hand, but modern kitchens use specialized conveyors for efficiency.
The combination of creamy cheese and tomato sauce creates a balanced flavor—sweet dairy tones down the acidity of the tomatoes.
The dish is frequently garnished with fresh basil or parsley for added brightness.
In the United States, “Stuffed Shells” are common on vegetarian menus, with meat replaced by plant‑based proteins.
A baked casserole version layers shells, sauce and cheese for an extra‑comfort twist.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: The cheese and meat filling provide complete animal protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Calcium and vitamin D
items.content: Parmesan and other cheeses are rich in calcium, supporting bone and dental health.

items.title: Lycopene in tomato sauce
items.content: Tomatoes are a major source of lycopene, an antioxidant linked to cardiovascular health.

items.title: Fiber from pasta
items.content: When whole‑grain shells are used, they add dietary fiber that aids digestion.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Meat and cheese supply B6, B12 and niacin, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: High calorie density
items.content: The dish is rich in fats and carbs, so portion control is advisable for weight‑managed diets.

items.title: Lactose and dairy allergy
items.content: Cheeses may trigger reactions in individuals with lactose intolerance or casein allergy.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Tomato sauces often contain added salt; low‑sodium versions are recommended for those with hypertension.

items.title: Meat safety
items.content: Undercooked ground beef can harbor pathogens; ensure the sauce reaches a safe internal temperature.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve hot, topped with fresh herbs and a sprinkle of grated parmesan. A drizzle of extra‑virgin olive oil or balsamic reduction adds extra flavor. Leftovers reheat well in the oven at 350 °F, covered with foil to keep the cheese moist.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the cooked dish in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. For longer storage, freeze in portion‑size containers for up to 2 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of 165 °F before serving.
